To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

lung cancer risk decreases gradually in former smokers with a smoking history of 30+ pack years as the number of years since quitting increases, and that a range of upper limits for years since quitting could be supportable for lung cancer screening.
lung cancer risk decreases with years since quitting smoking in 30+ year smokers.

lung cancer risk decreases gradually over time in former smokers with 15 or more years of cessation, but the risk is still 10 times higher than in never smokers after 30 years of cessation, and the lung cancer risk in 30+ year former smokers is 30 times higher than the lung cancer risk of never smokers, regardless of the number of years since smoking cessation.

lung cancer risk by years of quitting in smokers who have smoked for 30 years.
the relationship between lung and breast cancer and smoking.
the risk of lung cancer among smokers and former smokers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against screening for lung cancer with LDCT in former smokers who had quit more than 15 years ago, and that a range of upper limits for years since quitting may be supportable.
the lung cancer risk decreases gradually as YSQ increases in former smokers who have smoked 30+ pack years.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of lung cancer is not zero for 30+ packyear ex-smokers.
the risk of lung cancer in former smokers is not zero, even after 20 years of cessation, and that the risk decreases gradually with time since quitting.
lung cancer risk is not zero in 30+ year former smokers and that lung cancer screening should be offered to these individuals, but that the screening frequency should be reduced as YSQ increases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
lung cancer risk does not drop off sharply after 10–15 years of cessation.
the lung cancer risk of 30+ pack/year former smokers does not decrease linearly with YSQ, but decreases gradually, with risk remaining elevated for many years.
lung cancer risk decreases gradually over time in 30+ year pack smokers who quit.
